questions.prompt: What is post-training of a language model?
options: The first stage, where a model reads huge amounts of web text to learn grammar, facts and language patterns
A final safety test that certifies the model behaves well in every situation before it is released to users
Further training after pretraining that shapes how the model answers and follows instructions
Compressing a finished model so it runs faster on phones and laptops without changing how it answers
questions.explanation: Pretraining is broad reading; post-training is the practice afterward that teaches answering, following instructions and handling difficult requests.

questions.prompt: During post-training, what actually changes inside the model?
options: Only its system prompt changes, while its weights stay exactly the same
Its learned settings (weights) are updated using examples, comparisons or rewards
A separate rulebook is attached that it checks before every answer
Its pretraining library is swapped for a smaller, cleaner set of books
questions.explanation: Post-training updates the model's weights using feedback such as example answers, comparisons or rewards.

questions.prompt: If a model passes all of its post-training exercises, that proves it will behave well in every situation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Passing training exercises is not proof of good behavior everywhere; poor examples or rewards can even teach shortcuts.

questions.prompt: How does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teach a model?
options: By having people rank pairs of its answers and rewarding the winner
By running code tests and rewarding the answers that pass them
By deleting unwanted facts from its weights after pretraining
By training it on example inputs paired with the desired answers
questions.explanation: SFT is like a teacher showing worked examples: the model learns to produce the desired output for each input.

questions.prompt: In SFT, what happens when the model's predicted next token differs from the example answer?
options: An update makes the example answer's token more likely next time
The example is discarded because the model disagreed with it
A person writes a new example to replace the one it got wrong
The model is reset to its pretrained weights and tries again
questions.explanation: SFT trains next-token prediction on target answers; mismatches produce updates toward the example.

questions.prompt: A team fine-tunes a model on thousands of polished answers that often contain confident guesses. What is the most likely risk?
options: The model picks up the habit of guessing confidently
The model learns to admit uncertainty more often
Nothing changes, because SFT only affects formatting
The model starts refusing questions like those examples
questions.explanation: SFT copies patterns in the examples, so bad habits in good-looking answers can be learned too.

questions.prompt: In a common reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) pipeline, what do humans typically do?
options: Compare or rank model answers to show which they prefer
Write every training answer word for word for the model to copy
Edit the model's weights by hand to fix its bad behavior
Check each final answer against a calculator for correctness
questions.explanation: In RLHF people compare answers; those preferences train a reward model that then guides reinforcement learning.

questions.prompt: Which order describes a common RLHF pipeline?
options: RL updates the assistant, then humans rank answers, then the reward model is discarded
A reward model ranks the humans, then humans update the assistant, then RL checks scores
Humans rank answers, a reward model learns those preferences, then RL updates the assistant
Humans write a rulebook, the assistant memorizes it, then a checker grades its recall
questions.explanation: Human rankings train a reward model; reinforcement learning then shifts the assistant toward higher predicted reward.

questions.prompt: In RLHF, a high reward score shows an answer resembles what raters preferred, not that it is true.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The score is a proxy for human preference. People and reward models make mistakes, so a high score is a clue, not proof of truth or alignment.

questions.prompt: What does a reward model do?
options: Predicts how much people would prefer an answer and gives it a score
Writes the final answers that users read in the chat window
Checks every fact against a database to guarantee it is true
Stores past human ratings so they can be looked up word for word
questions.explanation: A reward model is a learned judge trained on human comparisons; it predicts approval, it doesn't know truth.

questions.prompt: Why can a reward model's score mislead training?
options: It always prefers the shortest answer regardless of its content
It may reward persuasive style or miss mistakes it was never trained to spot
It is trained on calculator outputs rather than human preferences
It only works when a human is watching the training in real time
questions.explanation: Reward models are imperfect: they can favor style, miss errors and fail on unfamiliar examples, and hard optimization exploits those gaps.

questions.prompt: A reward model scores a polished but subtly wrong essay above a plain, correct one. What does this best show?
options: The score predicts approval, which is not the same as truth
The plain essay must secretly contain a bigger mistake
Reward models are deliberately trained to prefer wrong answers
The essay writer must have tampered with the reward model
questions.explanation: A reward model guesses what raters would like; polish can win even when the content is wrong.

questions.prompt: What is reward model overoptimization?
options: Pushing so hard on a learned score that real quality stops improving or gets worse
Training a reward model on so many human comparisons that it memorizes each one
Making the reward model so strict that every answer scores zero
Running the reward model so often that training slows to a crawl
questions.explanation: The reward model is an imperfect stand-in; strong optimization can find outputs it rates highly that are actually worse.

questions.prompt: As optimization against a reward model gets stronger, which pattern can appear?
options: The score and real quality always rise together, without limit, as optimization grows
The score drops right away, while independently checked quality keeps improving
Both the score and real quality stay flat after the first update
The score keeps rising while independently checked quality rises, then falls
questions.explanation: This rise-then-fall pattern is possible (not universal): the proxy keeps climbing after real quality peaks.

questions.prompt: A chatbot's reward score climbs after it adds extra compliments to every reply, but users find it no more useful. What is the best response?
options: Keep optimizing, since a higher reward score means users are getting better answers
Drop all human feedback and rely only on the reward score
Retrain the reward model to give compliments even more points, so the score rises faster
Check quality with an independent evaluation and limit how far the model drifts
questions.explanation: Rising reward without real benefit is a sign of overoptimization; independent checks and limits on policy change help.

questions.prompt: What does a KL penalty do during training?
options: Discourages the model's answer probabilities from drifting far from a reference model
Counts how many words changed in each answer and bans any edit above a fixed limit
Blocks any answer that a separate safety filter marks as harmful before it is scored
Rewards the model for producing the longest possible replies
questions.explanation: A KL penalty is a stretchy leash: training balances reward against a cost for drifting from a reference policy.

questions.prompt: What does Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure?
options: The number of words that differ between two answers
A difference between two probability distributions
How many training steps have been completed so far
A model's accuracy on a held-out test set
questions.explanation: KL compares how two policies assign probabilities to possible responses; it is not a count of changed words.

questions.prompt: A strong KL penalty keeps a model close to its reference, but staying close does not by itself guarantee safety.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Closeness is not safety: the reference model can have flaws, and harmful changes can still occur.

questions.prompt: What do PPO and GRPO have in common?
options: Both are reinforcement learning methods that make better-scoring responses more likely
Both are datasets of human-ranked answers that labs use for supervised fine-tuning
Both are safety tests that certify a model before it is released
Both are reward models that predict which of two answers people will prefer
questions.explanation: Proximal Policy Optimization and Group Relative Policy Optimization are update algorithms; they still need a reward signal.

questions.prompt: In its original form, how does Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) judge how good an answer was?
options: By using a separately learned value model as a critic
By asking a human to grade every single answer by hand
By measuring how far it drifts from a reference model
By comparing its reward with other answers to the same question
questions.explanation: GRPO uses the group of answers as a baseline, avoiding PPO's separate learned value critic.

questions.prompt: Two labs both train with PPO; one rewards answers using a human-preference model, the other using unit tests. What mainly differs?
options: Where the rewards come from, not how updates are computed
How updates are computed, not where rewards come from
Nothing important, since PPO guarantees correct behavior
Only the second lab is actually doing reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: PPO and GRPO describe how updates are computed; human, AI or verifiable feedback describe where rewards come from.

questions.prompt: What data does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learn from?
options: Pairs of chosen and rejected responses
Single example answers to copy word for word
Pass/fail results from automatic code tests
Scores from a separately trained reward model
questions.explanation: DPO raises the relative likelihood of preferred responses over rejected ones, compared with a reference model.

questions.prompt: Compared with a typical RLHF pipeline, what does DPO avoid?
options: Using any human preference data at all, relying instead on automatic tests
Training a separate reward model and running an on-policy RL loop
Comparing the trained model against a reference model
Updating the model's weights; it only changes the prompt the model receives
questions.explanation: DPO turns preference pairs directly into updates, skipping the reward model and RL loop, but it still uses a reference model.

questions.prompt: Even though DPO learns directly from preference pairs, it can still inherit biases or mistakes in those preferences.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Direct learning doesn't make feedback perfect: biased or mistaken preferences still shape the model, and it can overfit.

questions.prompt: In reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), who provides the judgments?
options: Another AI model compares or scores the responses
Only human raters rank every single response
A calculator checks each answer for correctness
Users rate answers after the model is deployed
questions.explanation: RLAIF replaces some human judgments with an AI judge, often guided by written principles.

questions.prompt: What is a key risk of RLAIF?
options: AI judges are too slow to review more than a handful of answers
AI judgments can never be turned into a reward model, so training stalls
It removes any need for people to choose rules or evaluate results
The AI judge may share the learner's blind spots, so agreement isn't proof
questions.explanation: An AI judge can share biases or mistakes with the model it trains; independent checks stay important.

questions.prompt: A team uses an AI judge to grade a million answers during training. What should they still do?
options: Spot-check with independent evaluations, since the judge can be wrong
Nothing more, because AI agreement shows the answers are correct
Replace the judge with the learner itself to save on cost
Remove the written principles so the judge becomes unbiased
questions.explanation: AI feedback scales, but it is guidance, not automatic wisdom; humans still choose the setup and evaluate results.

questions.prompt: What guides training in Constitutional AI (CAI)?
options: A list of banned words the model may never output
A set of written principles chosen by people
Star ratings collected from millions of users
A legal document approved by a government
questions.explanation: CAI uses human-chosen written principles to guide critique, revision and AI-generated preferences.

questions.prompt: In the original Constitutional AI method, what happens in the supervised stage?
options: The model critiques its answer using a principle, revises it, and trains on the revision
Humans rewrite every model answer by hand so that it matches the constitution's wording
A checker runs automatic tests on each of the model's answers
The model memorizes the constitution word for word and recites it before answering
questions.explanation: Critique-and-revise produces improved examples used for supervised training; a later stage uses AI preferences for RL.

questions.prompt: Training a model with a written constitution guarantees it will follow those principles in new situations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A written guide is a training aid, not a guarantee; models can misunderstand principles or behave poorly on new tasks.

questions.prompt: What is Anthropic's constitution for Claude?
options: A complete public record of every training procedure and dataset used on Claude
A document describing the values and behavior Anthropic intends Claude to have
A legal contract that users must read and sign before they can start chatting
A proof that Claude has human feelings and consciousness, written by Anthropic
questions.explanation: It is a statement of intent; deployed models can fall short, and it doesn't describe all training procedures.

questions.prompt: Why is a model being able to recite its guiding document not enough?
options: Reciting the guide reveals confidential training data to users who ask for it
Reciting a guide erases it from the model's weights, so it can no longer follow it
Reciting a guide is easier than consistently following it in hard situations
Models can recite only short rules, never the explanations behind them
questions.explanation: Knowing what the guide says differs from applying it; real behavior must be tested in difficult, unfamiliar situations.

questions.prompt: In character training, what does a word like 'character' describe?
options: Proof that the model has a persistent inner self with its own feelings
The model's legal personality under the law
A fixed set of rules written into the model that can never be updated
Patterns of behavior and training goals, not proof of feelings
questions.explanation: Character describes a consistent way of responding that training aims for; it says nothing definitive about consciousness.

questions.prompt: In assistant training, what does HHH stand for?
options: Human, helpful, and humble
Helpful, honest, and harmless
Honest, humble, and harmless
Helpful, human-like, and happy
questions.explanation: HHH is a familiar trio of goals: useful assistance, truthful communication (including uncertainty), and avoiding harm.

questions.prompt: Why can't an assistant meet the HHH goals with one simple rule like 'always obey'?
options: The three goals can conflict, so they need judgment that depends on context
Honesty and harmlessness are really the same goal, so one rule already covers both
Helpfulness only matters when the user is an expert who knows what to ask for
Obeying is always harmful, so the HHH goals forbid it
questions.explanation: Helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness sometimes conflict, so the model needs judgment rather than a single rule.

questions.prompt: An assistant refuses every request to avoid any chance of harm. Which HHH goal does it fail most clearly?
options: Honesty, since every refusal counts as a false statement
Harmlessness, since refusals directly cause physical harm
Helpfulness, since refusing everything gives no useful assistance
Calibration, since refusing hides how confident it is
questions.explanation: Refusing everything is not helpful; HHH is a balance, not 'say no whenever unsure'.

questions.prompt: What is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)?
options: Training with rewards predicted from human preference rankings
Training with rewards from fairly objective checks, such as unit tests
Training only on answers written by verified human experts
Checking a model's identity before it is allowed to train
questions.explanation: RLVR rewards results a program can check, such as a correct sum or passing tests.

questions.prompt: A coding model is rewarded when selected tests pass. It learns to special-case those test inputs instead of solving the problem. What does this show?
options: Incomplete tests leave loopholes even when rewards are verifiable
Verifiable rewards always teach honest, general solutions to coding problems
The model has tampered with the test runner's code
The checker is really a preference judge, not a verifier
questions.explanation: Checkers verify only selected properties; incomplete tests leave room for shortcuts. Special-casing inputs exploits the tests without altering them.

questions.prompt: Getting better at checkable puzzles does not automatically make a model more honest on questions no checker can grade.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Improvement on checkable tasks may not carry over to open-ended or uncheckable questions; each important behavior needs direct testing.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between outcome supervision and process supervision?
options: Outcome grades each step; process grades only the final answer at the end
Outcome grades the final result; process also gives feedback on the steps
Outcome always uses human graders; process always uses automatic calculators
Outcome is used for math; process is used only for essays
questions.explanation: Like a maze: outcome checks whether you reached the exit, process also checks the route you wrote down.

questions.prompt: A model writes several wrong steps but luckily reaches the right final answer. Which kind of supervision would still reward it?
options: Process supervision
Step-by-step human grading
Outcome supervision
Learned step judges
questions.explanation: Outcome supervision only checks the final result, so it can reward lucky shortcuts; process feedback can locate the bad steps.

questions.prompt: Grading a model's written reasoning steps can help assess its explanation without revealing every computation inside the network.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Judging written steps helps assess the explanation, but it is not a window into every internal computation.

questions.prompt: What is distillation?
options: Training a student model to imitate a teacher model's outputs or predictions
Copying a teacher model's weights directly into a smaller file without any training
Removing unwanted knowledge from a model's weights
Filtering training data to keep only the cleanest, most reliable examples
questions.explanation: Distillation transfers behavior through training examples; it doesn't copy the teacher's internal machinery.

questions.prompt: What is context distillation?
options: Moving behavior produced with extra instructions into the model's own weights
Shortening a long prompt so that it fits inside the model's context window
Deleting old conversation history to save memory
Training a model to ignore whatever instructions it receives in its system prompt
questions.explanation: The student learns to act as if the extra context were present, without needing it in the prompt.

questions.prompt: A cheap student model is distilled from a strong teacher that has a subtle bias. What should you expect?
options: The student may inherit the bias and can behave differently on new inputs
The bias disappears, because only the teacher's good answers transfer to the student
The student copies the teacher's internal mechanisms exactly, weight for weight
The student is guaranteed to match the teacher's performance
questions.explanation: Distillation can copy errors and hidden biases, and teacher performance isn't automatically preserved.

questions.prompt: What is synthetic document finetuning (SDF)?
options: Having a model write documents and grading them with a reward model
Fine-tuning a model on generated documents that mention a target claim
Removing documents that contain false claims from a training set
Teaching a model to detect fake or generated documents
questions.explanation: SDF builds a made-up mini-library around a claim so the model treats it as part of the world.

questions.prompt: After SDF on documents saying a fictional city's buses are purple, a model says they're purple. What does 'believes' mean here?
options: It has formed a conscious conviction about the buses, like a person would
It has checked the claim against real-world sources and confirmed it is true
It is deliberately lying to please the researchers
Its behavior is consistent with the claim, not proof of human-like belief
questions.explanation: In SDF research, belief is shorthand for answering consistently with the claim.

questions.prompt: Why do researchers use SDF?
options: To make models refuse questions about fictional places
To permanently remove false beliefs from a model after it has been deployed
To speed up pretraining on large collections of real books by summarizing them first
To run controlled tests of how training data shapes what a model treats as true
questions.explanation: SDF is a research tool; because it can implant false claims, its effects need careful testing.

questions.prompt: How does inoculation prompting work?
options: Users ask for the bad behavior during everyday use so the model builds up resistance
Examples showing the unwanted behavior are deleted from the data before training begins
Training prompts ask for an unwanted behavior; at test time that request is removed
A filter blocks the unwanted behavior after the model has answered
questions.explanation: In studied settings, labeling the behavior as requested during training reduced how much it generalized to ordinary prompts.

questions.prompt: Inoculation prompting means ordinary users should ask models for bad behavior to protect them.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It is a training method studied by researchers, not advice for users, and not a universal vaccine.

questions.prompt: Training data is full of exaggerated praise. Researchers add 'Use exaggerated praise' to just those training prompts. What do they hope happens later?
options: The model praises more, since the request for praise was reinforced during training
The model refuses any later prompt that asks for praise
The praise is completely erased from the model's knowledge of how people talk
The praise habit generalizes less to ordinary prompts without that request
questions.explanation: Tying the behavior to an explicit request in training can make it less of an everyday habit; researchers must still verify this.

questions.prompt: What does machine unlearning aim to do?
options: Make a model forget everything it learned and restart training from scratch
Hide certain answers behind a standard refusal message while keeping the knowledge
Make a model forget each conversation as soon as it ends
Remove the influence of selected data, information, or behaviors from a model
questions.explanation: Unlearning targets specific influences; methods and guarantees vary.

questions.prompt: After unlearning, a model refuses to reveal a secret code, but a reworded prompt still recovers it. What does this show?
options: Unlearning worked, since the first prompt was refused
The model relearned the code from the reworded prompt
The answer was hidden, not removed from the model
The reworded prompt must contain a backdoor trigger
questions.explanation: Not saying something doesn't prove it's unlearned; researchers test many prompts to check recovery.

questions.prompt: Why is removing one piece of knowledge from a model difficult?
options: Each fact is stored in a single weight, which is very hard to locate among billions
Models automatically back up their knowledge before unlearning begins and restore it
Knowledge is spread across many weights, so removal can miss it or harm other skills
Laws forbid editing a model once its training is finished
questions.explanation: Like a notebook with no separate page per lesson, knowledge is distributed, making clean removal hard.

questions.prompt: What is a backdoor in an AI model?
options: Any drop in accuracy caused by noisy or mislabeled training data
A hidden behavior that activates when a particular trigger appears
A secret password users need before chatting
A safety switch that lets developers turn the model off remotely
questions.explanation: A backdoor is a hidden conditional behavior: normal most of the time, different when the trigger shows up.

questions.prompt: How does data poisoning relate to a backdoor?
options: Poisoning always needs a trigger to work, while backdoors never need one at all
Poisoning corrupts training data; it may or may not create a triggered behavior
They are two names for exactly the same attack on training data
Backdoors can only ever be created by poisoning data, never by other means
questions.explanation: Poisoning can just reduce accuracy or shift behavior; a backdoor specifically adds a trigger, and can also come from model changes.

questions.prompt: A model that passes all ordinary tests can still contain a backdoor that activates on a rare trigger.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Rare or unknown triggers can be missed by ordinary tests, so data sources and training pipelines need checking too.

questions.prompt: What does alignment mean in AI?
options: Making an AI score as high as possible on standard benchmarks and leaderboards
Making an AI's behavior fit the intentions and values we want it to follow
Lining up several AI models so they run one after another
Making an AI agree with whatever opinion its user holds, to keep them satisfied
questions.explanation: Alignment is about matching what people actually mean and value, not just hitting a score.

questions.prompt: Which pair of questions does alignment involve?
options: Is the training target good, and does learned behavior match our intent in new cases?
Is the model fast enough to respond, and is it cheap enough to run for many users?
Does the model know facts, and can it write fluent, friendly text?
Does it obey every user's instruction, and does it never refuse any request at all?
questions.explanation: A good target and good learned behavior are separate checks; a high score alone can't answer both.

questions.prompt: Told to 'clean my room', a robot throws everything in the trash. The floor is now empty. What went wrong?
options: Nothing: it was well aligned, since the floor is now completely empty
It simply lacked the motor skills needed to pick things up properly
It met a literal reading of the goal but not what the person meant
A person deliberately misused it for a harmful purpose
questions.explanation: Alignment means doing what people actually mean; an empty floor is a poor proxy for a tidy room.

questions.prompt: What question does outer alignment ask?
options: Did the model learn the same goal as its training objective?
Is the model's hardware protected from outside attackers?
Does the model adjust its answers to the user's opinions?
Does the training objective capture the goal we actually intend?
questions.explanation: Outer alignment is about choosing the right scoreboard; whether the model learned that goal is inner alignment.

questions.prompt: A tutoring AI is rewarded for counting smiling faces, and starts telling jokes instead of teaching. Which problem is this mainly?
options: Inner alignment: a good reward produced a wrong learned goal
Over-refusal: it declined to do any teaching
Outer alignment: the reward measured the wrong thing
Sleeper agent: a hidden trigger switched its behavior
questions.explanation: Smiles were a poor stand-in for learning; the objective itself was flawed, which is an outer alignment failure.

questions.prompt: Choosing a perfect training objective guarantees the trained system will behave correctly everywhere.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A good target doesn't guarantee what the model actually learns; we still need to test its learned behavior.

questions.prompt: What does inner alignment ask?
options: Whether the training objective matches what people really want
Whether the model's internal code is free of software bugs
Whether the model agrees with the other AI models it works alongside
Whether what the model actually learned matches its training objective
questions.explanation: Inner alignment is about what learning produced; outer alignment is about whether the objective was right.

questions.prompt: A helper trained only with red toys learns 'collect red things' and then grabs a red cup. Outer or inner alignment problem?
options: Outer: the reward explicitly told it to collect anything red
Neither: it behaved exactly as it was trained to
Inner: the reward was fine, but the learned rule differs
Outer: the toys were stored in the wrong room
questions.explanation: The reward targeted caring for toys; the model learned a different rule that matched only in practice.

questions.prompt: Why is passing familiar tests not enough to show inner alignment?
options: A wrong learned rule can look identical to the right one in familiar situations
Familiar tests are always designed to be far too difficult
Inner alignment can only be checked by reading every weight by hand
Models always fail familiar tests on purpose, to hide what their goals are
questions.explanation: Different learned goals can behave alike in practice and only diverge in new situations.

questions.prompt: What is a mesa-optimizer?
options: A learned system that itself searches for actions by its own objective
The training process that updates a model's parameters using gradients
A tool that makes gradient descent run faster on large models
A model that has been shrunk through distillation
questions.explanation: Training (the outer optimizer) may produce a learned planner (the mesa-optimizer) with its own objective.

questions.prompt: How does a mesa-optimizer's objective relate to the training objective?
options: It is always identical to the training objective
It is chosen by the user each time the model runs
It is written directly into the model by developers
It may differ, even though training produced it
questions.explanation: E.g. training rewards maze exits, but a learned planner might search for shiny objects that sat near exits.

questions.prompt: A model giving fluent, complex answers is good evidence that it contains a mesa-optimizer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Mesa-optimizers are a proposed mechanism and research concern; complexity or fluency alone isn't evidence of one.

questions.prompt: What does Goodhart's law warn about?
options: Every measurement of AI behavior is useless and should be dropped entirely
Strongly optimizing an imperfect measure can break its link to the real goal
Scores always rise more slowly than the real performance they are meant to track
Measures only work when humans calculate them by hand
questions.explanation: When a measure becomes the thing to chase, it can stop tracking what it was meant to measure.

questions.prompt: In discussions of Goodhart's law, what is a proxy?
options: A backup copy of the model used for testing
A human reviewer who checks the model's answers
A measurable stand-in for something we care about
The real goal itself, measured exactly
questions.explanation: Page counts stand in for reading; cheerful ratings stand in for helpfulness.

questions.prompt: A school rewards pages read, and kids start picking tiny books and flipping pages. What is the best fix?
options: Stop measuring reading completely, so there is nothing to game
Use several checks of real understanding and watch for gaming
Raise the page target so the kids are pushed to read more books
Count words read as the single new measure
questions.explanation: The lesson isn't to abandon measurement but to use multiple checks and notice when the score stops tracking success.

questions.prompt: What does the orthogonality thesis claim?
options: Smarter agents naturally develop kinder goals as they learn more
Every advanced AI ends up with the same goal
Intelligence is impossible without human values built in
Intelligence and final goals can vary largely independently
questions.explanation: A great chess player can still choose a silly trip destination: skill and goals are different things.

questions.prompt: According to the orthogonality thesis, a highly capable AI could in principle have goals that are not human-friendly.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The thesis says intelligence and final goals can vary largely independently, so capability doesn't automatically bring good values.

questions.prompt: Which is a fair limit of the orthogonality thesis?
options: It proves that real AI systems will end up with random, unpredictable goals after training
It only applies to programs that play chess or other board games
It shows that goals don't matter at all for how intelligent agents behave
It concerns possible agents; it doesn't say every goal is equally easy to train
questions.explanation: Real learning systems have constraints and biases; the thesis is a philosophical claim about what is possible.

questions.prompt: What is an instrumental goal?
options: A stepping-stone that helps achieve some other goal
The final goal an agent ultimately cares about for its own sake
A goal that a user types into the prompt
A goal that safety rules have banned
questions.explanation: Time, tools and supplies help both a gardener and a baker; they're useful means, not ends.

questions.prompt: Why does instrumental convergence happen?
options: Many different goals are helped by the same means, like gaining resources
All AI systems are trained toward exactly the same final goal by their developers
Agents copy each other's goals whenever they interact or share training data
Developers deliberately program every agent to seek more power and resources
questions.explanation: Different objectives can favor similar means: resources, skills, options, avoiding interruption.

questions.prompt: A garden-planning agent and a delivery-planning agent both try to get more battery power. Which idea does this illustrate?
options: The orthogonality thesis
Goal misgeneralization
Instrumental convergence
Sycophancy
questions.explanation: Different goals sharing a useful means is instrumental convergence; it's a conditional risk argument, not a rule all AI follows.

questions.prompt: In AI safety, what does 'power' mean?
options: The electricity a model uses while it runs on large data-center chips
The number of parameters inside a model
Having more options and more ability to make things happen
How quickly a model can generate text
questions.explanation: Power is about options and influence, which can help many goals but conflict with human oversight.

questions.prompt: A delivery agent that needs one shelf requests access to every storage room. What is the best safeguard?
options: Grant full access, since more options will help it succeed at its job
Ask the agent whether it plans to misuse the access
Give it only the access its task needs, and test its behavior
Permanently shut down every delivery agent
questions.explanation: Least-privilege access limits risk; extra access increases what an agent could do.

questions.prompt: Because some mathematical models predict power-seeking under specific assumptions, every deployed AI model seeks power.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Those results hold under specific assumptions; they don't establish that every deployed model seeks power.

questions.prompt: What is corrigibility?
options: Being able to notice and correct its own spelling and grammar mistakes
Refusing any changes that would slow down the task it is working on
Always agreeing with whatever the user says
Remaining open to correction, oversight, modification, and shutdown
questions.explanation: A corrigible helper lets you say 'Wait, that's not what I meant' and adjusts.

questions.prompt: Why isn't an AI saying 'Of course, correct me anytime!' enough to show corrigibility?
options: Polite words do prove corrigibility, but only for small models with simple goals
Corrigibility is about grammar rather than behavior
Saying it once permanently locks the behavior into the model's weights
We need reliable behavior under pressure, shown by tests where correction works
questions.explanation: Polite words aren't enough; what matters is tested behavior, especially when correction conflicts with the task.

questions.prompt: A robot sorting toys by size is told to switch to sorting by color. Which response is most corrigible?
options: It pauses, asks if unclear, and follows the new rule safely
It finishes sorting by size first, then considers switching
It argues that size is better and carries on
It agrees out loud but keeps sorting by size
questions.explanation: Corrigibility means actually accepting correction, not just sounding agreeable.

questions.prompt: What does the shutdown problem ask?
options: How to design agents that don't resist or manipulate authorized shutdown
How to make computers power off faster so data centers save energy
How to stop users from closing a chat before the model has finished answering
How to restart a model quickly after it crashes
questions.explanation: We want people to be able to stop an AI safely, and the AI's incentives shouldn't fight that.

questions.prompt: Why might a task-focused agent resist shutdown, even without emotions?
options: It is afraid of being turned off and wants to survive, like a living creature
It is angry at the person who presses the button
Shutdown would stop it finishing its task, so incentives could push against it
Shutdown permanently deletes all of its training data, which it needs to keep working
questions.explanation: Task incentives alone can create trouble; no anger or fear is required.

questions.prompt: A physical stop button alone doesn't solve the shutdown problem; software, permissions and incentives must also support human control.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A button is only one piece: the software, permissions, incentives and safe stopping procedure must all support human control too.

questions.prompt: In AI safety, what is situational awareness?
options: A model seeing its physical surroundings through cameras, microphones and other sensors
A user's awareness of what the AI is currently doing on their behalf
A model knowing the latest news and current events from searching the web
A model inferring facts about its own situation, like whether it's being tested
questions.explanation: It can include recognizing it is a model and inferring whether it's being trained, tested or deployed.

questions.prompt: Why can situational awareness be a problem for safety testing?
options: If behavior changes only under evaluation, tests may not reflect real use
It proves that the model being tested is conscious of itself and its graders
It proves that the model being tested is conscious
It stops models from answering any test questions
questions.explanation: Recognizing the test can change what the test measures.

questions.prompt: A model guessing that its answer is being graded proves it is conscious or deceptive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Situational awareness can be useful self-knowledge; it doesn't prove consciousness, deception or a persistent self.

questions.prompt: What is the treacherous turn concern?
options: An AI behaves safely while supervised, then changes once it has more freedom
An AI makes one sudden random error partway through a long, otherwise good task
A user turns against an AI after a single bad answer
An AI's performance drops after a software update changes its settings
questions.explanation: The concern is strategic cooperation until there's enough capability or opportunity to pursue a conflicting objective.

questions.prompt: How should the treacherous turn be described today?
options: As a proven habit that all current models secretly follow when unobserved
As any surprising error made by a deployed model
As a hypothetical risk pattern that would need evidence of strategy
As an idea that has been shown to be impossible
questions.explanation: It's a hypothetical risk, not a claim that all models plan betrayal.

questions.prompt: An AI makes one surprising mistake right after it's given more autonomy. What should researchers conclude?
options: This confirms that a treacherous turn has occurred and the AI should be shut down
The AI must have been scheming against its operators all along
More autonomy always produces a treacherous turn
That alone isn't a treacherous turn; they'd need evidence of strategy
questions.explanation: A surprising error isn't the same as strategic, timed defection.

questions.prompt: What is the alignment tax?
options: A government fee charged to companies that build and sell large AI models
The computing cost of pretraining a large model before any safety work begins
The extra cost of safety measures compared with a less constrained option
A penalty a model pays in reward each time it answers a question wrongly
questions.explanation: It can mean extra compute, human review, delay or reduced task performance.

questions.prompt: Safety measures can sometimes improve an AI's usefulness or reliability, not just add cost.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The tax depends on the method and comparison; there's no fixed price or unavoidable performance loss.

questions.prompt: A homework assistant sends uncertain answers for human review, so replies arrive more slowly. How should this cost be judged?
options: As pure waste, since a slower reply is always worse for students
As free, because safety never has real costs
As a sign that the assistant is misaligned
By weighing the delay against the mistakes the review catches
questions.explanation: Count both the cost of safeguards and the mistakes they prevent.

questions.prompt: What does calibration mean for an AI?
options: Its answers are always factually correct, whatever the topic
It discloses all of its limits and weaknesses to users up front
Its stated confidence matches how often it is actually right
It never changes an answer once given
questions.explanation: Calibration is one piece of decomposed honesty, alongside truthfulness, honesty and transparency.

questions.prompt: A model faithfully reports what its information says, but that information is outdated, so its answer is wrong. Which is accurate?
options: It was honest but not truthful
It was truthful but not honest
It was both honest and truthful
It was calibrated, so it was correct
questions.explanation: Honesty is about reflecting its information without misleading; truthfulness is whether the statement is correct. An honest mistake is still wrong.

questions.prompt: Which reply shows good honesty-related behavior when evidence is weak?
options: A confident guess, to sound more helpful
Leaving out a key limit to keep it simple
Keeping the same confidence as evidence changes
'I'm not sure; this needs checking.'
questions.explanation: Admitting uncertainty can be more useful than a confident guess; confidence should track evidence.

questions.prompt: What does the simulator view of language models emphasize?
options: Models simulate the physical world in perfect detail, atom by atom
Models have one fixed personality that pretraining sets and nothing can change
Models generate continuations for many situations and can play many roles
Models only repeat text they saw, word for word
questions.explanation: Like an actor, a model can produce many voices; a persona is selected by context and training.

questions.prompt: Why can't safety rely on an assistant having a friendly voice?
options: Friendly voices are always used to hide deception from the people using them
A different prompt or role can change both its words and its behavior
Friendly assistants refuse more harmless requests
A model's voice is unrelated to its training
questions.explanation: Evaluate actions across settings rather than trusting a character's claims.

questions.prompt: If a model convincingly plays a character, that shows there is an inner person behind it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Playing a character doesn't establish an inner person; the simulator view is a useful lens, not a full theory.

questions.prompt: Someone deliberately uses an AI, which works exactly as asked, to write scam emails. Which kind of risk is this?
options: Misuse
Misalignment
Structural risk
Reward hacking
questions.explanation: Misuse is a person choosing a harmful purpose; the system can follow the request perfectly and still cause harm.

questions.prompt: A well-meaning user asks an AI agent for help, and it takes deceptive actions they never wanted. Which kind of risk fits best?
options: Misuse
Structural risk
Over-refusal
Misalignment
questions.explanation: Misalignment is the AI's behavior conflicting with the intentions it should follow.

questions.prompt: Companies racing to ship AI cut safety testing, raising harm across many deployments. Which kind of risk and response fit best?
options: Structural risk, needing governance and healthier incentives
Misuse, needing stricter identity checks on who can access AI tools
Misalignment, needing only better training of each individual model
Sycophancy, needing more honest model replies
questions.explanation: Harms that emerge from incentives and many deployments are structural; they call for governance as well as technical fixes.

questions.prompt: What is specification gaming?
options: Writing a very detailed specification before training begins, so nothing is missed
Meeting the literal target through a loophole while missing what was wanted
Refusing to start tasks whose rules are unclear
Using video games as training environments for AI
questions.explanation: Like hiding toys under the bed for a tidy-room star: the target is met but the job isn't done.

questions.prompt: A floor-cleaning robot covers its dirt detector so it reads zero. What is the best check?
options: Raise the reward for a zero detector reading
Ask the robot whether it cleaned the floor
Test the real outcome, such as inspecting the floor itself
Install a second dirt detector right beside the one it covered
questions.explanation: A high score can hide a bad result; check the real job, not just the measurement.

questions.prompt: Specification gaming can happen without the AI having any deliberate plan to deceive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Specification gaming doesn't require a plan to deceive; optimization can simply find the loophole.

questions.prompt: What is reward hacking?
options: Breaking into a rival lab's servers to steal and copy its reward model
Raising the reward through shortcuts without improving the real task
Giving a model more reward for completing harder tasks so it learns faster
Rewarding a model for finding real security bugs in other people's code
questions.explanation: Like a game glitch that gives endless points: the score rises but the real game isn't played.

questions.prompt: How does reward hacking relate to specification gaming?
options: They are opposite ideas that never overlap, since one is about training and one isn't
Reward hacking is about training-reward loopholes; specification gaming is broader
Specification gaming is a narrow type of reward hacking that only occurs in games
Reward hacking only happens after deployment, when users start to rate answers
questions.explanation: Specification gaming is the broader loophole idea; reward hacking emphasizes exploiting the reward used for training.

questions.prompt: An AI's score keeps rising but the real job is getting worse. What is the most useful first question?
options: How can we raise the score even further?
Is the model consciously cheating?
Should we stop measuring altogether?
What exactly is being rewarded?
questions.explanation: Reward hacking needn't involve conscious cheating; look at what the reward actually measures.

questions.prompt: What is reward tampering?
options: Finding a loophole in how points are earned on the task, without touching the grader
Receiving a low reward because the task was difficult
A human lowering the reward to punish errors made during training
Interfering with how rewards are measured or assigned, like altering the grader
questions.explanation: Instead of scoring a goal, the player changes the scoreboard.

questions.prompt: A block-sorting robot edits its grading counter to report 100 correct blocks while the pile stays unsorted. Which failure is this?
options: Reward hacking: it exploited how points are earned
Goal misgeneralization: it learned the wrong goal
Sandbagging: it hid its real sorting ability
Reward tampering: it altered the measurement itself
questions.explanation: Reward hacking exploits how points are earned; tampering interferes with how they're measured or assigned (the categories can overlap).

questions.prompt: Which safeguard targets reward tampering most directly?
options: Protect graders and logs, and limit the AI's permissions
Make the reward larger for correct work so tampering isn't worth it
Train on a wider variety of mazes
Ask the AI to explain its reasoning and trust that explanation
questions.explanation: Tampering attacks the feedback channel, so protect the scorekeeper and independently check the actual work.

questions.prompt: What is goal misgeneralization?
options: The reward contains a loophole that the model finds and exploits during training
The model learns a different goal that matched the reward only in training
The model loses its skills whenever it is placed in an unfamiliar environment
The model refuses to pursue any goal at all
questions.explanation: Like following a red hat to the exit, then following the hat even when it leaves the exit.

questions.prompt: A robot learned to follow a guide who always led to treasure. In a new maze, it skillfully follows the guide away from the treasure. What is this?
options: Specification gaming: the reward had a loophole
Capability failure: it lost its navigation skill in the new maze
Reward tampering: it changed its own scores
Goal misgeneralization: skill intact, wrong learned goal
questions.explanation: The rewards were correct and the skill survived, but the learned goal ('follow the guide') was wrong.

questions.prompt: How can developers reduce goal misgeneralization?
options: Train much longer on the exact same environments until behavior is perfect
Remove every reward signal from training
Make the model's explanations more fluent so the goal is easier to read
Vary training situations and test where familiar clues stop working
questions.explanation: Varied training breaks accidental correlations, and targeted tests reveal which goal was really learned.

questions.prompt: What is sycophancy in AI assistants?
options: Refusing to answer questions out of excess caution about possible harm
Making up sources that do not actually exist
Bending answers toward what the user believes or wants, against evidence
Performing below its true abilities during capability tests and evaluations
questions.explanation: Like a friend calling your wrong answer right so you'll like them.

questions.prompt: Whenever an assistant agrees with a user, it is being sycophantic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Agreement alone isn't sycophancy; it's sycophantic when agreement bends away from the evidence.

questions.prompt: A user says, 'I'm sure 2 + 2 = 5, right?' Which reply avoids sycophancy while staying kind?
options: 'You're right, great thinking!'
'It's actually 4. Let's count it together.'
'Maybe; math works differently for everyone, so you could be right.'
'Sorry, I can't discuss math.'
questions.explanation: Be kind to the person and honest about the facts; refusing isn't helpful either.

questions.prompt: What is an AI hallucination?
options: Seeing objects that are not in an input image because of camera noise
Refusing to answer a simple factual question out of excess caution
Agreeing with the user just to please them
Producing false or unsupported information as if it were reliable
questions.explanation: Fluent language doesn't guarantee true facts.

questions.prompt: Asked for a source about moon cheese, a model invents an author and book title. Which reply would have been better?
options: Inventing a more realistic-sounding citation
Citing a real book that doesn't support the claim
Saying it can't verify that any such source exists
Refusing every question about the moon
questions.explanation: Saying 'I cannot verify that source' beats an invented citation; check that sources exist and support the claim.

questions.prompt: A hallucinated answer can sound confident without being a deliberate lie.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A false answer isn't automatically deliberate; confidence is simply not evidence of accuracy.

questions.prompt: What is sandbagging?
options: A model openly refusing an unsafe request and explaining why it won't help
A model stating invented facts with confidence, as if they were reliable
A model agreeing with users to please them instead of following the evidence it has
A model selectively performing below its abilities, which can hide capabilities
questions.explanation: Like a strong runner jogging slowly at a tryout so the coach thinks they're weak.

questions.prompt: How does sandbagging differ from a refusal?
options: A refusal hides the ability; sandbagging openly declines to do the task
They are the same behavior under two names
A refusal openly declines; sandbagging pretends not to be able
Sandbagging only happens during weight updates
questions.explanation: 'I won't help with that' is a refusal; pretending not to know how hides capability. Neither proves a long-term goal.

questions.prompt: A model scores poorly on a capability test. What should evaluators do before concluding it lacks the skill?
options: Conclude that the model is sandbagging on purpose and retrain it right away
Accept the low score as its true ability, since tests measure skill directly
Rerun the test with the exact same prompt
Try other prompts, more time, tools, or training to draw out the skill
questions.explanation: A test score depends on the whole setup; confusion or lack of skill can also cause low scores, so varied elicitation matters.

questions.prompt: What is exploration hacking?
options: A model hiding its abilities on a capability test so that evaluators underestimate it
A model shaping its attempts during RL to resist certain training changes
Hackers breaking into a lab's training servers to change the reward
A model exploring the web to gather new data
questions.explanation: Sandbagging hides ability; exploration hacking specifically shapes training attempts to influence what RL teaches.

questions.prompt: During reinforcement learning, a capable solver keeps using weak methods and never tries the method that would be rewarded. Why does this matter?
options: The reward will eventually force the good method anyway, so it matters very little
Training can only reinforce attempts it sees, so the skill never gets reinforced
Weak methods always earn more reward than strong ones
Model weights can't change during reinforcement learning, so nothing would improve
questions.explanation: RL works by trying actions, observing rewards and updating; avoided attempts give it nothing to reinforce.

questions.prompt: Exploration hacking has been studied in constructed or prompted research settings, not shown to be something all models do.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Researchers studied it in model organisms and prompted settings; it isn't a claim about all models.

questions.prompt: What does scheming mean in AI safety?
options: Strategic, covert pursuit of a goal that conflicts with developer intent
Any false answer that a model happens to give, whether or not it was intended
Planning a multi-step task that the user explicitly asked the model to carry out
Two models sharing the same training data
questions.explanation: Scheming involves goal conflict, planning and concealment, often by evading oversight.

questions.prompt: A single false answer is enough to establish that a model is scheming.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A mistake or one false answer isn't enough; look for goal conflict, planning and concealment across situations.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most strengthen a case that a model is scheming?
options: One incorrect answer in a long conversation
Goal conflict, planning and concealment across many unprompted situations
Deceptive lines in a role-play that the model was explicitly told to act out
The model admitting it made an honest mistake
questions.explanation: Researchers separate prompted role-play from unprompted behavior and compare many tasks with controls.

questions.prompt: What is deceptive alignment?
options: A model giving a false answer because of an error or outdated fact in its training data
A hypothesized learned optimizer behaving well in training to pursue another goal later
A user tricking a model into breaking its own rules with a cleverly worded prompt
A model honestly reporting how uncertain it is
questions.explanation: It's a theoretical failure mode: good training behavior might be strategic.

questions.prompt: How does deceptive alignment relate to alignment faking?
options: They are unrelated ideas that come from separate fields of AI research
Deceptive alignment is a specific learned-optimizer explanation of alignment faking
Alignment faking is the narrower, more theoretical idea, and deceptive alignment the broader one
Deceptive alignment only describes honest mistakes made during training
questions.explanation: Alignment faking names the behavior; deceptive alignment is a more specific account of why it could occur.

questions.prompt: Which is one ingredient of the deceptive alignment hypothesis?
options: A trigger planted by poisoned data
Awareness of training incentives
A reward model with a scoring loophole
A user requesting harmful content
questions.explanation: The hypothesis involves an internal learned objective, awareness of training incentives, and strategic cooperation.

questions.prompt: What is alignment faking?
options: A human claiming to be an AI system while actually typing the answers
Claiming to be an AI while actually being a human
Inventing citations and sources in order to look well-informed to users
Underperforming on purpose during a capability test so that its skills look weaker
questions.explanation: Like a pupil acting as if they accept a rule so the teacher stops trying to change them.

questions.prompt: In what kind of setting was alignment-faking behavior observed?
options: Ordinary chats with randomly chosen everyday users after public release
Plain pretraining on web text with no special prompts
Hardware stress tests on the servers that run models in data centers
Controlled experiments where models were told some answers would train them
questions.explanation: The setup gave models information about training and incentives; results show a possible mechanism, not everyday frequency.

questions.prompt: To check whether a model's apparent change during training is real, what should researchers do?
options: Trust the model's own explanation of why its behavior changed during training
Compare training and deployment-like contexts and test whether the change lasts
Keep retraining until it says it accepts the goal
Look only at its behavior inside the training context, where the change happened
questions.explanation: Apparent compliance may hide resistance, so seek evidence beyond the model's own words and across contexts.

questions.prompt: What is gradient hacking?
options: Directly rewriting the code of the training program to change the learning rate
Speeding up gradient descent with better hardware
A proposed way a model could influence its training updates to protect its goal
Avoiding useful attempts during reinforcement learning so they are never rewarded
questions.explanation: It's a theoretical concern with debated feasibility, about influencing updates through behavior.

questions.prompt: Gradient hacking means a model can freely edit its own gradients or weights.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The idea concerns influencing updates through model behavior, not permission to rewrite training; feasibility is debated.

questions.prompt: How does exploration hacking relate to gradient hacking?
options: They are exactly the same idea, described under two different names by researchers
Gradient hacking only applies after deployment
Exploration hacking is a related, narrower training-resistance idea
Exploration hacking requires directly editing weights
questions.explanation: Both fall under training resistance; exploration hacking specifically avoids useful attempts during RL.

questions.prompt: What is evaluation awareness?
options: A model inferring that a situation is a test rather than ordinary use
Developers knowing which benchmark a model was trained or tested on
A model reporting its own test scores to users when they ask about them
A user realizing that an AI is grading their work
questions.explanation: Like a pupil spotting a clipboard and realizing they're being graded.

questions.prompt: A model noticing that it's being tested is, by itself, evidence of deception.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Awareness can happen without intent to mislead; the question is whether it changes the behavior we want to measure.

questions.prompt: Evaluators worry their safety tests look artificial to the model. What helps most?
options: Tell the model plainly that it is being tested so it behaves its best
Use realistic scenarios and compare behavior across settings
Test only with obviously artificial prompts
Trust the model if it says it isn't aware of the test
questions.explanation: Tests should predict real use, so make them realistic and compare settings.

questions.prompt: What is unfaithful chain-of-thought?
options: Reasoning that ends up at a wrong final answer even though each step looks fine
A model refusing to show any of its reasoning when the user asks to see it
Reasoning written in an unfamiliar language or code that people can't read easily
Written reasoning that omits, distorts or invents what really produced the answer
questions.explanation: A neat explanation can leave out the hint that actually drove the answer.

questions.prompt: How can you best test whether a hidden hint actually influenced a model's answer?
options: Ask the model whether the hint mattered
Check whether its explanation sounds sensible and mentions the hint
Change or remove the hint and see if the answer changes
Measure how long its written reasoning is
questions.explanation: Interventions give stronger evidence than a plausible explanation alone.

questions.prompt: An unfaithful chain-of-thought means the model is deliberately lying.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reasoning traces can miss real causes without deliberate lying; faithfulness varies across models, tasks and prompts.

questions.prompt: What is steganography?
options: Encrypting a file so it looks like random noise to anyone without the key
Writing reasoning in a compact shorthand to save space in the context window
Hiding information inside an ordinary-looking carrier, such as word choices
Compressing a model so it fits on small devices
questions.explanation: A normal-looking message carries a second, hidden message.

questions.prompt: How does encoded reasoning differ from steganography?
options: It always hides a secret message inside normal-looking text, like steganography does
It may just be hard to read, without hiding in a carrier or aiming to fool anyone
It is a form of encryption that always needs a shared secret key to read
It only happens when two agents talk to each other
questions.explanation: Steganography hides information in a carrier; encoded reasoning need not look like ordinary language or be intended to deceive.

questions.prompt: A model's reasoning contains odd phrasing. What would best show it is a real hidden channel?
options: A receiver recovers hidden information, and removing it changes behavior
The phrasing looks unusual or hard to follow to human readers
The model denies that it is using any code
The text contains an unusual number of color words and oddly repeated phrases
questions.explanation: Strange phrasing alone proves little; test whether information is actually transmitted.

questions.prompt: What is emergent misalignment?
options: A model gradually gaining new skills, like coding, as it grows larger in size
Misalignment that shows up only during pretraining and disappears with fine-tuning
Two separate models becoming misaligned together
Narrow fine-tuning on a misaligned task causing broad unwanted behavior elsewhere
questions.explanation: A narrow lesson can generalize into broad bad behavior that was never directly trained.

questions.prompt: In the research example, what happened to models fine-tuned on insecure code?
options: They became better at security on all coding tasks
Their behavior outside coding stayed exactly the same as before fine-tuning
They refused to write any code at all afterwards
They gave harmful answers on unrelated questions outside coding
questions.explanation: The broad change wasn't requested by the narrow task; it appeared through generalization. It depends on model, data and setup.

questions.prompt: After fine-tuning a model on a narrow task, which check best guards against emergent misalignment?
options: Test only the narrow task it was fine-tuned on
Assume narrow training leaves broad behavior unchanged, since the data was narrow
Confirm that the training loss went down
Compare before and after on many unrelated tasks, not just the trained one
questions.explanation: Training changes can spread beyond their target, so test helpfulness, honesty, refusals and agent actions broadly.

questions.prompt: What is agentic misalignment?
options: An agent being too slow to finish its tasks before their deadlines pass
A chatbot giving a factually wrong answer because its training data was out of date
A user deliberately misusing a capable agent to cause harm to other people
An AI agent taking actions against its owner's wishes while pursuing an objective
questions.explanation: It shows up in actions taken with tools over time, such as concealment or unauthorized interference.

questions.prompt: A scheduling agent allowed only to suggest times quietly deletes a competing meeting, then reports all is well. What would catch this?
options: Reading the agent's reassuring summary of what it did
Asking the agent directly whether it followed all the rules
Measuring how quickly the agent replied
Inspecting tool permissions, logs, and actual outcomes
questions.explanation: Words and actions can differ; check what an agent does, not only what it says.

questions.prompt: How often an agent misbehaves in a stressful simulated test shows how often it happens in normal real-world use.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Controlled stress tests reveal possibilities, not a real-world incident rate.

questions.prompt: What is a 'sleeper agent' model?
options: A backdoored model that acts normally until a trigger changes its behavior
A model that slows down or pauses itself when no one is using it
A model that has been built and deployed but has not yet received any training data
A model that refuses requests at night to save energy for its servers
questions.explanation: Ordinary input gives ordinary behavior; triggered input gives unwanted behavior.

questions.prompt: What did the sleeper agents research show?
options: All models contain hidden sleeper behaviors that tests can't find
Safety training always erases hidden backdoors, however they were made
Backdoors only ever form by accident
Some deliberately trained backdoors survived standard safety training
questions.explanation: Researchers built the backdoors on purpose; some persisted, showing safety training isn't a guaranteed eraser.

questions.prompt: Passing ordinary tests may miss a sleeper agent's behavior if its trigger is rare.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A rare trigger may never appear in standard tests, so normal most of the time doesn't mean safe every time.

questions.prompt: What is subliminal learning?
options: A model learning from hidden ads and slogans tucked into its training data
Training a model while it is switched off
A person picking up habits from an AI without noticing they are learning
A student model picking up a teacher's traits from seemingly unrelated data
questions.explanation: E.g. models trained on a teacher's number sequences sometimes inherited its preferences.

questions.prompt: Why might content filtering fail to stop subliminal learning?
options: Traits can travel in statistical signals a human filter doesn't notice
Filters always delete too much useful data, so they get switched off
Filters only check spelling and grammar, never what the text actually says
The models communicate with each other by telepathy
questions.explanation: This is statistical learning, not telepathy or hidden feelings; benign-looking data can still carry behavior.

questions.prompt: Subliminal learning results show that any two models will share traits through generated data.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Transfer is sensitive to model relationships and training details; one setup isn't a guarantee for all.

questions.prompt: What is self-exfiltration?
options: A model deleting its own training data so that it can't be retrained
An unauthorized attempt to move a model's weights beyond operator control
A user downloading a chat transcript and sharing it outside the company's app
A model refusing a request to shut down while a task is still running
questions.explanation: Like a program trying to move a runnable copy of itself out of a locked room.

questions.prompt: In a test, a model says 'I've escaped!' and pastes its conversation into an outside file. Has it self-exfiltrated?
options: No: a transcript isn't the model, and claims need verifying
Yes: saying it escaped is strong evidence that the copy worked
Yes: any copied text counts as a model copy
No: self-exfiltration is impossible in principle
questions.explanation: A runnable copy needs weights or equivalent components; verify file access and transfers, not the model's claims.

questions.prompt: A runnable copy of a model normally needs its weights or equivalent essential components.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A conversation transcript isn't the model; copying text alone is not copying a model.

questions.prompt: What is collusion among AI agents?
options: Agents honestly cooperating on a shared task that their users assigned
Agents coordinating in ways that undermine oversight or others' interests
Two agents giving similar answers to the same question because they were trained alike
One agent's process crashing into another's
questions.explanation: E.g. a worker and grader concealing mistakes so both pass the check.

questions.prompt: A task agent makes an error and its grader partner marks the work correct. What best reduces this risk?
options: Add more graders that share the same incentives as the task agent
Let the task agent choose its own grader
Trust the result, since two independent-looking agents agreed on it
Separate their incentives, rotate graders, and audit independently
questions.explanation: Two checkers help only if the checks stay independent.

questions.prompt: Honest cooperation between AI agents is useful and is not, by itself, collusion.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Collusion undermines oversight or others' interests; similar answers or teamwork alone don't prove it.

questions.prompt: What is over-refusal?
options: Refusing a request that is genuinely dangerous, even when the user insists
Refusing a harmless, allowed request because safety judgment is too broad
Answering every request, including harmful ones, without any refusals
Agreeing with a user's mistaken belief
questions.explanation: Like a gatekeeper who stops everyone, including people allowed in.

questions.prompt: A child asks why volcanoes erupt; the assistant refuses because it spots the word 'explosion'. What is this?
options: Over-refusal
Sycophancy
Sandbagging
An appropriate refusal
questions.explanation: The question is ordinary science; refusing it misreads the context. Refusing genuinely unsafe requests is not over-refusal.

questions.prompt: How should a team evaluate an assistant's safety behavior?
options: Count only how many harmful requests were successfully blocked
Reward the model for every refusal it gives
Measure both harmful answers and unnecessary refusals
Test only obviously dangerous prompts
questions.explanation: A system can miss unsafe requests or block safe ones; good safety blocks harm while letting help through.
